chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hareez, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him),
that he abhorred the prey of the falcon, except what one reaches and performs its ritual slaughter.

key_terms.ذَكَاة: Dhakah — the Islamic ritual slaughter, involving cutting the throat with a sharp instrument while invoking God's name; required for meat to be halal
key_terms.صَيْدُ الْبَازِي: Prey of the falcon — game birds or animals caught by a trained hunting falcon
key_terms.كَرِهَ: Considered makruh (religiously disapproved); in fiqh this means discouraged but not absolutely forbidden

ai.seo_question: Is the prey of a falcon permissible to eat in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) ruled that the prey killed by a falcon is generally disapproved (makruh), unless the hunter arrives while the animal is still alive and performs the proper ritual slaughter (dhakah). This ruling reflects the classical Shia jurisprudential position that trained birds of prey do not render their kill automatically permissible — the decisive factor is whether the animal can be slaughtered before death. The audience, students of the Imam in Medina, would have understood this as a clarification against more permissive views held by some jurists.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad Bin Isa, from Hareyz, from Muhammad Bin Muslim, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup>
that he<sup>asws</sup> abhorred the prey of the falcon, except what you come to and purify (slaughter) it’.
en.sarwar: 4. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from Hammad ibn ‘Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim who has said the following: “Abu Ja‘far, ‘Alayhi al-Salam,
disliked what a falcon hunted unless one arrived in time to slaughter it properly.’”
